data.targetWord: An error caused by code that breaks the grammatical rules of the programming language; the program cannot run at all because the interpreter rejects the code before execution.

examples.en-GB: A missing colon after an if statement — if score > 50 — causes a syntax error.

data.targetWord: An error that occurs during program execution, causing the program to crash; the code is syntactically correct but performs an illegal operation such as dividing by zero.

examples.en-GB: result = 10 / 0 causes a ZeroDivisionError runtime error when the program runs.

data.targetWord: An error where the program runs without crashing but produces incorrect output due to a flaw in the algorithm or conditions.

examples.en-GB: Writing average = total + 3 instead of total / 3 is a logic error — the program runs but gives the wrong answer.

data.targetWord: The process of finding and correcting errors (bugs) in a program, using strategies such as trace tables, print statements, and IDE debuggers.

examples.en-GB: Debugging the program revealed a logic error where the loop ran one iteration too few.

data.targetWord: An error in a program that causes it to behave incorrectly, either by crashing or by producing wrong output.

examples.en-GB: The bug in the code caused every score to be calculated 10 marks too high.

data.targetWord: The specific inputs used when testing a program to check that it produces the correct outputs.

examples.en-GB: For a program accepting ages 11–18, test data would include the values 11, 14, 18, 10, and 'abc'.

data.targetWord: Typical, valid inputs that the program is designed to handle under expected everyday conditions.

examples.en-GB: For a program accepting ages 11–18, an age of 14 is normal test data.

data.targetWord: Inputs at the very edge of the valid input range, including the minimum value, the maximum value, and values just outside these limits.

examples.en-GB: For a program accepting ages 11–18, the boundary values to test are 10, 11, 18, and 19.

data.targetWord: Invalid inputs that the program should reject or handle gracefully without crashing, such as text entered where a number is expected.

examples.en-GB: Entering "hello" when the program expects a number is erroneous test data.

data.targetWord: A structured table used to document planned tests, recording the test type, input, expected output, actual output, and whether the test passed or failed.

examples.en-GB: A test table for an age validator would include columns: Test #, Type, Input, Expected Output, Actual Output, Pass/Fail.

data.targetWord: The output that a correctly working program should produce for a given input, determined before the test is run.

examples.en-GB: For an age validator with input 15, the expected output is 'Valid age'.

data.targetWord: The output that the program actually produces when run with a specific test input, which is then compared against the expected output.

examples.en-GB: If the actual output differs from the expected output, the test has failed and a bug must be found.

data.targetWord: A table used to manually track the value of every variable at each step of a program's execution, helping to identify where a logic error first occurs.

examples.en-GB: A trace table for a loop would have columns for the loop variable i and any other variables that change each iteration.

data.targetWord: A marker set in an IDE debugger that pauses program execution at a specific line, allowing the programmer to inspect variable values at that point.

examples.en-GB: Setting a breakpoint at line 10 pauses the program so you can check what values the variables hold at that moment.

data.targetWord: A debugging technique where temporary print() statements are inserted at key points in the code to display variable values as the program runs, helping to pinpoint where a value first goes wrong.

examples.en-GB: Adding print("total =", total) inside a loop reveals what the running total is at each iteration.

data.targetWord: A built-in tool in an Integrated Development Environment that allows programmers to step through code line by line, watch variable values change in real time, and set breakpoints.

examples.en-GB: Using the IDE debugger in Thonny, a student stepped through their loop and discovered the counter was not resetting correctly.

data.targetWord: Checking that user input meets the required criteria before the program uses it, for example checking that a number is within an acceptable range.

examples.en-GB: Validation checks that an entered age is between 11 and 18 before accepting it.

data.targetWord: Python's term for a runtime error; an event that disrupts the normal flow of the program and causes it to crash unless the exception is handled.

examples.en-GB: ZeroDivisionError, IndexError, TypeError, and ValueError are all examples of exceptions in Python.

data.targetWord: Text output by the Python interpreter when an error occurs, indicating the type of error and the line number where it happened.

examples.en-GB: The error message 'IndexError: list index out of range' at line 7 helps the programmer find the fault quickly.

data.targetWord: A document that describes all the tests to be carried out on a program, specifying what data will be used and what the expected outcomes are for each test.

examples.en-GB: A test plan for a login system would include tests for correct passwords, wrong passwords, and empty input.

data.targetWord: An input or situation at the extreme ends of what a program might encounter, often where bugs are most likely to occur.

examples.en-GB: Testing a list-sorting program with an empty list or a single-element list represents edge cases.

data.targetWord: A testing approach where the tester has full knowledge of the program's internal code and structure, and designs tests based on how the code works.

examples.en-GB: White-box testing lets the developer write tests that target each conditional branch in the code.

data.targetWord: A testing approach where the tester has no knowledge of the internal code and tests the program purely based on its inputs and expected outputs.

examples.en-GB: A user testing an app without seeing the source code is performing black-box testing.

data.targetWord: Re-running all previous tests after a bug fix or code change to ensure that the fix has not introduced new bugs elsewhere in the program.

examples.en-GB: After fixing the login bug, the team ran regression testing to check that the change had not broken the password reset feature.

data.targetWord: Checking that a program has been built correctly according to its specification, asking 'Did we build it right?'

examples.en-GB: Verification checks that the code does what the design document specified, not just that it runs.

data.targetWord: When a program terminates unexpectedly due to a runtime error, stopping execution before completing its task.

examples.en-GB: The program crashed with a ValueError when the user typed their name instead of a number.

data.targetWord: A correction made to the code that resolves a bug, restoring the program to correct behaviour.

examples.en-GB: The fix was to change range(1, 10) to range(1, 11) so that the loop correctly counted up to 10.

data.targetWord: The detailed error output Python produces when a runtime error occurs, showing the sequence of function calls that led to the error and the line number where it happened.

examples.en-GB: Reading the traceback carefully showed that the IndexError originated in the calculate() function at line 23.

data.sentence: A syntax error prevents the program from ____ at all.
A runtime error causes the program to ____ during execution.
A logic error produces ____ output without crashing the program.
Testing can demonstrate the ____ of bugs, but it cannot prove a program is completely bug-free.
Boundary data tests values at the ____ of the valid input range.
Erroneous data should be ____ by the program rather than causing a crash.
Normal test data represents typical ____ input that the program is designed to handle.
A test table includes columns for test type, input, expected output, actual output, and ____.
Accessing an index that does not exist in a list causes a(n) ____ runtime error.
Converting a non-numeric string to an integer with int("hello") causes a ____.
The hardest type of error to find is a ____ error because Python gives no error message.
A ____ table is used to manually track variable values as each line of a program executes.
A missing colon after an if statement is an example of a ____ error.
Dividing a number by zero causes a ____ runtime error in Python.
After fixing a bug, ____ testing re-runs all previous tests to check no new bugs were introduced.
For a program accepting ages 11–18, the value 10 is ____ test data.
For a program accepting ages 11–18, an age of 14 is ____ test data.
For a program accepting ages 11–18, entering the text "abc" is ____ test data.
In ____ testing, the tester has no knowledge of the program's internal code.
A program that runs to completion without crashing is not necessarily ____ because it may contain a logic error.
When a test fails, the actual output ____ the expected output.
Setting a ____ in an IDE debugger pauses program execution at a specific line.

data.title: Debugging a Program That Crashes
data.instruction: Put these steps in the correct order to debug a program that produces a runtime error.
items: Run the program and observe the error message and traceback
Read the error message to identify the type of error and line number
Examine the code at and above that line to understand what went wrong
Make a correction to fix the identified bug
Run the program again and test with relevant test data to confirm the fix works

data.title: Designing a Test Plan
data.instruction: Put these steps in the correct order to design a systematic test plan for a program.
items: Identify the valid input range and any constraints for the program
Choose normal test data — typical valid inputs the program should accept
Choose boundary test data — values at the minimum, maximum, and just outside the valid range
Choose erroneous test data — invalid inputs the program should reject
For each test, write down the input and the expected output before running the program
Run the program with each test, record the actual output, and mark each test as pass or fail
